title: API incident quickreference for responders (timeouts, 429s, streaming degradation, error spikes)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, responder-focused quickreference for on-call engineers handling common API degradations: client timeouts, surge 429s, degraded/patchy streaming, and elevated 5xx error rates. It is intentionally pragmatic — steps you can run in the first 10/30/60 minutes that isolate cause, limit blast radius, and keep customer surfaces alive.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to Redwood public API endpoints and primary edge layer and runtime clusters.
- Assumes standard SRE access (k8s, observability, rate-limiter consoles, deployment controls).
- Not a full postmortem — use this for first-response and temporary mitigations.

Key indicators to check immediately (first 2 minutes):
- Alert channels: Pager duty alert text, service name, sample error.
- Grafana quick checks: API 95p latency (1m/5m), request rate, 5xx rate, 429 rate, stream disconnect rate.
- Load/traffic: total inbound QPS and per-route QPS. Sudden spike vs gradual increase matters.
- Deployment/rollouts: are any canaries or rollouts active in the last 30 minutes? (check deployment history)
- Upstream/backing services: redis/memcache error rates, database failover events, model-serving pool health.

Quick dashboards/queries (copy-paste friendly):
- Total requests (1m): sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m])) by (route)
- 95p latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, route))
- 5xx ratio: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))
- 429 ratio: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status="429"}[1m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total[1m]))
- streaming disconnects: increase(stream_disconnects_total[5m]) by (route)

First 10 minutes (rapid containment):
1) Validate the alert and scope: which routes/endpoints, what percentage of traffic, how many customers impacted.
2) Identify if this is traffic-related or internal error: compare QPS vs normal baseline for the route.
3) If 429 spike and traffic surge: enable emergency throttles or burst caps in the edge rate-limiter to protect upstream (prefer short 1–5m windows).
   - Quick action: toggle rate-limiter to per-customer soft-limit or reduce global burst token bucket size.
   - Command (example): curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $RL_TOKEN" "https://rl-control/api/v1/policies/edge/adjust" -d '{"route":"/v1/generate","burst":50,"window_s":60}'
4) If timeouts or elevated 5xxs: shift traffic away from suspect deployments (pin to older revision) or scale runtime pool.
   - If canary is active and shows higher error rate -> immediately pause rollout and redirect traffic to previous stable revision.
5) For streaming degradation: switch streaming endpoints to short-poll fallback where possible (client-side config) and enable graceful chunking on runtime to reduce in-flight memory.

Triage checklist (by symptom):
A) Timeouts (client-side or edge):
- Confirm timeout type: client TCP timeout vs application-level (504) vs proxy-level.
- Check upstream latency (model runtime queues, kernel-level stalls). Look at pod-level p95/p99 CPU and GPU utilization.
- If pod-level backpressure: restart affected pods in a controlled manner (drain+restart one at a time) to avoid thundering herd.
- If persistent queueing: increase worker count temporarily or enable emergency burst capacity on Dedicated pools.
- Short-term mitigations: reduce max token limit per request, temporarily disable expensive features (structured-output heavy postprocessing).

B) 429s (rate-limited responses):
- Determine origin: edge rate-limiter vs upstream service returning 429s.
- If edge: check recent policy changes, quota resets, or a misconfigured token.
- If many unique clients hitting limits: soft-throttle by client tier (delay lower-tier requests) and open a traffic-shed window for 1–5 minutes.
- If upstream returns 429: identify which service (model-serving, cache) and apply same protections upstream (backoff, queue cap).

C) Degraded streaming (partial frames, high reconnects):
- Check connection-level metrics (connection churn, average chunk latency).
- Inspect edge logs for websocket/proxy errors (502, 504, 499 client closed).
- If problem concentrated on a region/hardware: failover streaming to alternate region or fallback to polling.
- Apply temporary limits: reduce max concurrent streams per client or enable small chunk sizes.

D) Elevated error rates (5xx spikes):
- Split errors by code and route. If a single route -> likely app code or a dependency. If many routes -> infra or platform degradation.
- Check control plane (k8s control errors, etcd flaps), storage latencies, and model-serving pool health.
- Consider rolling back recent infra changes or pausing autoscaler.

Safe operational commands (examples):
- k8s rollout pause: kubectl rollout pause deployment/api-frontend -n prod
- Restart single pod safely: kubectl drain pod/<pod> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data && kubectl delete pod/<pod>
- Scale runtime pool: kubectl scale deployment/runtime-pool --replicas=40 -n runtime
- Edge throttle toggle (example API): curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $RL_TOKEN" https://rl-control/api/v1/policies/edge/temporary-override -d '{"route":"/v1/chat","limit_per_min":1200,"duration_s":300}'

Mitigation decision tree (quick):
- Is this causing customer-facing failures? Yes -> contain and route away from suspect nodes, communicate. No -> continue investigation and monitoring.
- Is the root likely external traffic surge? Yes -> throttle at edge. If not, is there a recent deploy? Yes -> rollback/pause.
- If hardware saturation (GPU/CPU): scale/evacuate workload to burst pool or route to Dedicated cluster.

Rollbacks and canary pauses:
- If canary shows >x2 baseline error rate or >5% absolute delta in success rate -> pause/rollback immediately. Use automated policies in Console when available.
- Prefer progressive rollback: remove canary traffic, then scale down canary daemonsets, then redeploy stable image.

Communications (on-call → incident lead / customer success):
- Short message template for Slack (first 10 mins): "SRE: Investigating elevated [timeout/429/stream error] on /v1/* since 14:03 UTC. Impact: ~12% of requests. Applying temporary throttles and pausing recent canary. Will update in 15 mins. PD: <link>"
- After containment: note customer-facing mitigation (throttle, rollback) and ETA for full recovery.

When to escalate to paging L4/engineering:
- If degradation >15 mins without clear mitigation or no improvement after containment actions.
- If data plane is saturated (cannot scale), and traffic-shaping will cause >10% loss for paying customers.

Post-incident handoff notes (for follow-up checklist):
- Preserve logs and traces for the incident window (slice 15 minutes pre-alert to 60 minutes post containment).
- Export Grafana panels used during triage and attach to the incident ticket.
- Capture a list of short-term mitigations performed and their duration.
- Create follow-up actions: root-cause deep dive, test improvements for rate-limiter rules, broaden chaos tests for streaming stability.

Safety and guardrails:
- Avoid cluster-wide restarts unless absolutely necessary. Prefer targeted pod restarts.
- Prefer throttling over wholesale IP block unless malicious activity is confirmed.
- Document every temporary change as a ticket and set a TTL (auto-revert) if possible.

Examples of small experiments to add to SRE backlog (post-incident):
- Automated circuit-breaker that detects rapid p95 increase and proactively sheds non-critical traffic.
- Adaptive streaming chunking that reduces chunk sizes when per-connection latency crosses threshold.
- Canary health gating that checks real traffic success rate rather than only probe responses.

Appendix: quick checklist for responders (one-line items)
- Identify scope (routes, customers)
- Check for recent deploys/canaries
- Confirm traffic patterns (sudden spike vs slow ramp)
- Decide containment: throttle, rollback, or scale
- Apply mitigation with TTL and document in ticket
- Communicate short status to stakeholders
- Monitor metrics for 15/30/60 min windows
- Create post-incident follow-ups and assign owners

Notes/to-self (draft ideas):
- Consider a tiny CLI that wraps common toggles (rate-limiter/policies, canary pause, scale commands) with safe defaults and audit logging.
- Need a playbook page in Confluence linking to this quickreference and full runbooks for each subsystem (edge, runtime, model-serving).

Last edited by Ethan Chen.
